title: The Pastons Defend Their Home
text:
The Pastons were a gentry family in Norfolk, in eastern England, who rose from peasant origins to wealth in the fifteenth century. They kept their letters, and about a thousand of them survive, an unmatched record of an ordinary family's life during the Wars of the Roses.

The men were often away in London, fighting lawsuits over land. At home, the wives ran the estates. In 1448 Margaret Paston, wife of John Paston, was living in a house at Gresham, a manor claimed by a powerful neighbor, Lord Moleyns. In January 1450, according to the family's own complaint, Moleyns's men, a large armed force, broke into the house while she was inside, undermined the walls and carried her out. Earlier, as the threat grew, Margaret had written to her husband with practical requests: crossbows, poleaxes and almonds and sugar.

The family kept fighting through the courts. In 1459 John inherited Caister Castle from the old soldier Sir John Fastolf, and the inheritance was challenged. In 1469 the Duke of Norfolk besieged Caister with a small army. The young John Paston held out for weeks with a handful of men. Margaret wrote urgently to her eldest son, warning that the defenders were short of gunpowder and arrows and that his brother's life was in danger. The castle was surrendered, but the family eventually got it back.

The letters show a family bound together by duty, quarrels, money and stubborn courage.
lesson: Ordinary families have always had to defend what is theirs, and the steady person at home often does the hardest part. Keeping records and keeping together are both forms of strength.
people: Margaret Paston, John Paston I, John Paston II, John Paston III, Lord Moleyns
source: The Paston Letters, ed. James Gairdner (1904); Norman Davis, Paston Letters and Papers of the Fifteenth Century (1971 to 1976)
